Riley Rendezvous

By: Kate Barry | Paid

Proposal


Show:

One Liner (Tonight on Carte Blanche...):
110 years old and still going strong - Riley vintage cars on safari.

Summary:
In 1905 the first Riley automobile was manufactured in England. Now a group of local enthusiasts, joined by 3 cars being shipped over from abroad, will enjoy another Riley Rendezvous.

Further information:
Roy Jones is building up a completed Riley replica in his Bryanston workshop to be ready for the rally. The group will meet in Broederstroom on 10 October, and then embark on a motoring safari which taks them to Cullinan, Kaapsehoop, the Kruger national Park, Pilgrim's Rest, Dullstroom and back to Broederstroom.

Extra Budget Items:
Travel to Pilgrim's Rest, accommodation in Pilgrims' Rest for producer and cameraman.

Press Release:


Riley Rendezvous
A joyride, in every sense of the word, the Riley Rendezvous takes us on a road trip like no other. Carte Blanche joins a band of happy-go-lucky Riley owners on an epic and colourful journey through some of the most beautiful parts of South Africa.


Script:


RILEY RENDEZVOUS


V/O: Welcome to the Riley Rendezvous - a vintage car tour like no other. Every 3 to 4 years this group of enthusiasts cranks up their engines, applies a bit of spit and polish and sets off on the roads of South Africa to see the sights and show off their pride and joy.

Julian: I saw it advertised and thought this seems like a wonderful op0p0ortunity to use a Riley car in South Africa, which is a wonderful country.

V/O: Julian Riley is one of three owners who shipped their cars out from England for the event. The precious cargo arrived in Cape Town in September and was then sent up to Johannesburg by train. They were accompanied by two other cars from Cape Town, all eager to join the safari.
Mike Martin was on the platform to receive his special, one-of-a-kind Riley Sprite. It is the only model like this left in the world.

Mike: Early in 1937 Riley was looking to replace the Lynx, and they sent this car to a specialist bodybuilder, which was Tickford, Simon Tickford of Newport- Pagnell. They sent 2 cars, this being one of them. The other one is lost, not known of, the whereabouts not known.

Derek: You’ve owned this vehicle for quite a few years?

Mike: I have 35 years. People have admired it everywhere it goes. It’s a pretty little motorcar. It’s unique.

V/O: The group bravely set off from Park Station into the Joburg traffic. They were no sooner on the M1, when Julian’s car ran out of fuel. The sight of a Riley broken down at the side of the road would become a recurring theme on the tour, but help is always at hand. In no time at all the gracious lady was up and running and back on the road to the home of local Riley expert Roy Jones.


Roy: The price of one of these cars in the 1930s when they sold them, was around about 350 Pounds. So it was a good, middle of the range motorcar, well engineered and they had a very good reputation.

V/O: Riley was a British motorcar manufacturer that produced its first model in 1905. They went on to make saloons, coupes, tourers and sports cars. Later incorporated into British Leyland, the last Riley was produced in 1969.

Roy: In the 30’s there was a competition to see who could drive from Cape Town to Johannesburg the quickest, and of course a little Riley 9 1100 cc was the car that won it.

V/O: Roy spends 5 days a week in his workshop maintaining and rebuilding his cars. He built this Riley TT Sprite racing car from scratch, and every year it wins the Knysna Hill Climb.

Roy: Of the cars that enter at Knysna, it’s by far the quickest car in the country with a pre-war engine in it.

V/O: In fact there are only a handful of people who own Rileys in South Africa.

Roy: Probably between all of them there are about 20 or 25 cars in the country.

V/O: The Riley Rendezvous kicked off in Broederstroom and travelled through some of the old Transvaal mining towns: Cullinan, Kaapsehoop, Pilgrims Rest and Dullstroom. The cars weren’t allowed into Kruger Park as most of them have soft tops.

Derek link: I’d like to introduce you to Doris, the oldest Riley on the Rendezvous. Now they say you should never discuss a lady’s age, but I can tell you she was born in the late 1920’s.

Anthony: Doris is a 1928 Riley WD9, horsepower with twin overhead cam engine. Four doors, four speeds, and top speed is probably about – downhill with the wind behind you – 60km per hour.

Derek: Now the WD stands for War Department.

Anthony: Doris was built specifically for a contest for the British War Department after the First World War when they wanted new staff cars. So Morris, Austin and the Riley were in the running. An army captain drove it from England to Rhodesia as it then was, to demonstrate its reliability.

Derek: And that’s where you found Doris, in Zimbabwe?

Anthony: I did yes, because she stayed there. But they lost the contract to Austin.


Derek link: I’ve been wanting to do this for a long time. Gentlemen start your engines!


V/O: Doris led the procession of Rileys through the hills of Mpumalanga on the journey from White River to Hazyview. Coasting past the pine plantations it became clear that these grande dames move at quite a lick. Soon it was time to fill up.

Derek: Are these thirsty beasts?

Bob: Not really, depending on the vehicle and the size of the engine they are not too bad on fuel. You probably get about 15kms per litre, so not too heavy.

Derek: Sometimes you have to add something to the fuel though?

Dave: Yes lead replacement petrol is not that great, so we do add a lead additive in just to help the engine with a bit of lubrication.

V/O: While some of the Australian visitors found the local arts and crafts enchanting…

Visitor: They’re lovely.

V/O: …Some of the locals felt the same about their cars.

Local: Chatter – to boots.

V/O: But admiring looks are to be expected when owning a Riley according to John Allison.

Derek: John you call her The Princess.

John: Yes. It’s proper name is a Riley 2-seater RMB. But when my wife first saw it – and my wife has quite an eye for what I bring home – some of the cars I’ve bought in the past she said I don’t like that. But this one she was absolutely enamoured with from first sight. She said oh that’s a beautiful car. I think it has something to do with the colours or whatever it is that women like. This seems to be like a chick magnet, this thing.

Derek: I wanted to get behind the wheel, but the Riley owners aren’t too keen. They say these cars are out of motorplan – by about 80 years or so, or more.

Julian: I think Riley made cars for guys who are 5’8”, or 5’ 9”, but Derek you’re rather taller than that so I think you need to sit in the passenger seat.

Derek: Nice air-conditioning…

V/O: It was a perfect Sunday morning as the group set off for Pilgrim’s Rest. Julian Riley had just completed a rally in Portugal and was enjoying the rugged African landscape. There were 11 Rileys on the tour, with various models ranging from 1928 through to 1960. But we soon realized that once the bug has bitten, one Riley is never enough.

Julian: I have a Riley Sprite and I co-own a Riley Mentone with my father, which is a 6 cylinder car.

Anthony: I have four Rileys.

Deek: Now how many Rileys have you got?

John: Uh wait a minute… five I think, yes five.

Derek: Five?

John: Yes.

Mike: I have seven of them.

Derek: Now you’ve got 11 Rileys?

Phil: Yes.

Derek link: For most of these enthusiasts collecting vintage cars and driving them on these outings is a hobby, but if you pick the right model it can also be a lucrative investment.

Dave: Some of the more expensive Rileys here are probably worth in the region of 60 to 80 000 pounds. And the market there for the more expensive ones is definitely going to be in the UK or Europe.

V/O: Making good time the Riley Safari headed up and over Robber’s Pass just in time for tea. But as majestic as the scenery may be, coming safely down a mountain is not a cut and dried affair.

John: I watch my brakes on every downhill to make sure I’m going to stop if I need to.

Anthony: The one thing about Doris is if you want to stop, you’ve got to plan ahead. Don’t make any sudden decisions to stop because it won’t work.

Derek link: It’s a charming scene as the vintage Rileys potter along the roads of Mpumalanga. But it belies the hours and hours that are spent just keeping them in running order….take that for example.

V/O: The inevitable breakdown seemed to be welcomed as a chance for the guys to get their hands dirty.

Roland: If you can move that another inch I’d be very happy.

V/O: A sweeper vehicle followed the Rileys, but every time there was a problem they seemed to have enough spare parts and expertise to get the cars back on the road.

Derek: So you say you don’t need my help John?

John: There is a support vehicle standing by, this is half the fun.

Derek: To do it yourself?

John: To do it yourself, but sometimes it gets a bit painful.

Phil: Cars break down at the side of the road. You help them fix it, they help you fix yours if there’s a problem, and they do become lifelong friends.

V/O: The oldest driver on the Safari albeit in an MG – was 92 year-old Stewart Cuninghame, with his 87-year-old wife Thelma.

Derek: I notice there are not too many women at the wheel here?

Stewart: No there are women that actually drive cars and their husbands do the navigating, because I think the male is always the better navigator than the female. Now have I said the right or the wrong thing?

Thelma: I’m not so sure about that.

V/O: Stewart also races vintage motorcycles, and is a legend on the annual Durban Johannesburg rally.

Derek: And you still do them, or you did one at the age of 90?

Stewart: 91 yes. I’ve just retired from the DJ rally.

Thelma: He did it for 23 years, every year.

Derek: Now I guess you need a lot of time or money?

Thelma: Yes.

Stewart: Well I wouldn’t say a lot of money, because I’ve had a very economical wife. So we’ve saved a lot of money. Yes, we’ve been married 63 years next week.

Derek: What are you going to do in your old age?

Thelma: We hadn’t thought about that yet, because we still feel young.

V/O: Stewart and Thelma left Pilgrim’s Rest to catch up with the Rileys. After negotiating the infamous Lydenburg potholes, it was onwards and upwards to the highlands of Dullstroom. With almost a thousand kilometers under the fan belt, the Rileys were still going strong and ready for the next Rendezvous.
